item.title: Back to Afterschool Meltdowns
item.description:
Neurodiversity

Back to Afterschool Meltdowns

How to support neurodivergent kids who experience afterschool meltdowns or shutdowns.

Posted August 17, 2026

Key points
  • Many neurodivergent children and teens experience meltdowns and shutdowns after school each day.
  • Schools are not responsible for what happens outside of the school setting, leaving parents without supports.
  • Parents and schools can work together to set up accommodations that support success in multiple settings.
Source: RDNE Stock project / Pexels

This is the time of year when families prep for the new school year. There is both excitement and dread while school supplies are purchased, new outfits are chosen, and back-to-school events are attended. For many families of neurodivergent children, preparations are also being made for how to best handle the inevitable meltdowns or shutdowns that occur each day after school.

These meltdowns stem in part from the transition of going from summer break to a new school year. Students have new teachers, new classmates, new routines, and new expectations that can cause stress and anxiety. For many of these kids, there is also a daily buildup of anxiety as they work to mask, or make efforts to hide their neurodivergent traits, all day in school, only to have the stress of this result in either an explosion or implosion when they get home to their safe spaces.

Afterschool meltdowns/shutdowns are stressful not just for the individual, but for their family. I have sat with many children over the years, working to help them navigate those stressful afterschool transitions. I have also sat through IEP/504 meetings where families shared the distress of these daily afternoon meltdowns or shutdowns. While parents are usually met with sympathy, they are also inevitably told that what happens at home is not the school’s responsibility.

While it is true that the school is not responsible for what happens in other environments, the system we have created that includes a series of siloed supports leaves families scrambling to piece together resources and strategies during the times when those supports are not available. This is not helpful, and ignores that fact that while the meltdowns and shutdowns may not occur at school, they are very much caused by what happens in the school setting.

What Can Be Done to Support Neurodivergent Kids Across All Settings

Finding strategies that support children across the environments they exist in is important for their overall health and well-being. Supporting kids is everyone’s responsibility, regardless of whether an adult is part of their natural or professional support system. Here are a few ideas that both parents and schools can put in place that may help support children who struggle with after school meltdowns or shutdowns.

  • For parents, set up a routine for your child that they can look forward to that allows them to have space and downtime, to have their sensory needs met, or to do whatever else they need after a long school day. Encourage your child to be part of setting up a routine that works for them. If they are not able to do this, look for signs that the routine is working or not working for them.
  • Parents can ensure that their child has space and materials to work through their primary stress response in a health way. For example, if they tend toward their fight response, give them space for physical activity. If they tend toward their flight response, give them physical space to calm down. If they tend toward their freeze response, give them time for crafting, playing music, or other activities that allow them to dissociate in a healthy way. (For more, see my book, What’s Your Anxiety Level?).
  • Make sure to take kids to open houses and to request additional visits before school begins to meet teachers and staff and find classrooms before school starts. Let middle- and high-school students walk to their classes to practice figuring out where they are located before there are other kids in the building. Knowing what to expect will likely help decrease stress during the back-to-school transition.
  • For schools, it may be helpful for elementary-age children to have an extra break in the afternoon that provides activities that can allow a child to let out some of the anxiety that has been building up over the course of the day. This break should be taken daily, even if the child seems like they do not need it. The goal is to be proactive, not reactive.
  • Schools can also pay attention to settings that might be contributing to stress such as noisy lunchrooms. If a lunch space is overstimulating, let the child eat in an alternative setting. Another stressful space is the school hallway during passing periods. Letting students leave class and transition a few minutes early to avoid the busiest part of this time may be helpful. Remember to attend to children who heavily mask in front of peers and look for signs that they may be distressed such as irritability, not talking to others, becoming overly energetic, or other signs that may indicate hidden stress.
  • Schools can give children jobs to help avoid boredom like passing out tests, or taking notes to the office. This will limit stress for children who struggle with downtime.
  • Do not take away recess as a punishment. All children need their recess, but this is even more true for neurodivergent children. Removing their only break sets them up for failure.
  • For middle- and high-school age children, it may be helpful to schedule more difficult classes in the mornings and easier classes in the afternoon. Study hall in the afternoon may also be helpful.
  • Middle- and high-school students will also likely benefit from alternating nonpreferred and preferred courses during the school day as much as possible.

While many supports for neurodivergent children are siloed, their needs are not. Using perspectives such as systems theory or person-in-environment theory, which consider the whole person and encourage collaboration and cooperation between systems, will help set neurodivergent children up for success and ensure that more afterschool time is spent engaging in positive activities, rather than in severe stress responses that they have been working to bottle up all day. While what happens outside of school may not be the school’s responsibility, the entire child’s support system shares the goal of setting them up for success. With collaboration and a few accommodations throughout the day, families and educators can help make that success happen.

item.title: Why Your Healthcare Provider May Be Better Than My Blog
item.description:
Health

Why Your Healthcare Provider May Be Better Than My Blog

Your health needs more than good information.

Posted August 17, 2026

Key points
  • The internet knows a lot about health—but it doesn’t know you.
  • Even excellent research can obscure when people don't fit the pattern.
  • What helps most other people may be ineffective—or harmful—for you.
  • Read the science, then bring better questions to a healthcare provider who can see the whole picture.

My blog posts always include a caveat: Ask your healthcare provider before following this advice. That isn’t just a skip-over disclaimer or the grown-up version of “Don’t try this at home.” I mean it sincerely: Don’t change your health behaviors just yet.

What Scientific Articles Do and Do Not Do

The information in this blog is important. I spend weeks verifying science in every post, reading journal articles, and sometimes including co-authors with expertise on the topic.

An effective healthcare recommendation for any individual, however, should be individualized. Healthcare needs to consider your particular circumstances, not what’s right for the norm. Mr. Rogers was right: You are special.

The best medical and psychological research identifies patterns among different behaviors and physical health (in scientific lingo: associations between variables). Any given study may include a large range of people and well-designed comparisons.

But no one participant is likely to be your age, your sex, have your social activity, and also share your life history. Some studies exclude people based on medical conditions or health behaviors. Other studies took place in one location that differs from yours in terms of weather patterns, traffic, or environmental toxins.

Here’s a hypothetical study. My students often get sluggish and can’t pay attention after lunch. Imagine an intervention to improve their attention in my afternoon seminar. I assign them to go for 5- to 20-minute walks after lunch. They take an attention test in class to see if the walk had an effect.

The graph shows how those hypothetical scores might look. If this were true, the longer students walked, the more attentive they became. It looks like walking before class could improve their ability to pay attention and get better grades.

Hypothetical Study of Walking and Attention in Class
Source: Karen Fingerman with ChatGPT

Even the Best Intervention Won’t Work for Everyone

But if you check that graph again, you will notice the orange exceptions. Two of the students were less attentive than usual after the walk! One of them had an injury, and the walk exacerbated their pain. The other had already walked several miles to campus on the hottest day of the semester. (Keep in mind these are hypothetical students; I would not do this to my real students). I hypothetically apologized profusely to both.

Note that another student only walked for 10 minutes, but was one of the most attentive. That student had walked to their favorite coffee shop and ordered a double espresso. In this case, coffee may be the key factor. The point is that we don’t know. Don’t go out and drink espressos.

What Can You Do to Get at Healthcare for You

My hypothetical walking intervention didn’t get at the health issues you may care about most: how to prevent dementia, how to live longer in better health, or how to feel less lonely. You may be worried about a new symptom and whether an advertised medication will work for you.

Here are some things to keep in mind in seeking information.

Avoid Clickbait

Every day, a new exciting study claims it will prevent dementia, help you look better, or help you live longer. If the finding is too good to be true: It is too good to be true.

Be suspicious of certainty and dramatic promises. Medicine is full of probabilities and tradeoffs; claims of a “cure,” “secret,” “detox,” or one simple solution that works for everyone deserve extra scrutiny.

Check Expertise

Online influence is not scientific expertise. I use Reddit, LinkedIn, Yelp and other sources of crowdsourced input, but not for decisions about health or treatments. (Still not a TikTok viewer). Check the author’s relevant expertise, and whether they are selling a product, supplement, program, or subscription connected to their claims.

Some of the best information is a little dull. Government agencies responsible for public health typically have more accurate information than other websites: their URLs end in .gov.

Respected professional associations like the American Psychological Association or the American Medical Association have up-to-date information.

Google Scholar also gives quick access to information that medical professionals and researchers use. The journal articles can be challenging to read, but your body and healthcare are complicated, too.

Look for Evidence from Multiple Studies

Look for replication, not the exciting single study. A new study often gets the headline. Make sure that several studies have found that same thing. If only one study finds it, other researchers may find something different later.

Bring Questions to a Healthcare Professional

Diagnosis comes before treatment. Online information may accurately describe a treatment for a disease, but similar symptoms can have very different causes.

You can do things while waiting to see a doctor. Keep notes on symptoms, timing, severity, medications/supplements, and what makes things better or worse—useful information to bring to the appointment.

Balance what you learned on the web with trust in your healthcare provider. Ask questions! Ask your healthcare provider what they think is happening, what evidence supports the recommendation, what the alternatives are, and what uncertainties remain. You can even share what you’ve read online to get input on its accuracy.

Focus on broadly health-supporting basics. Prioritize sleep, physical activity, nutritious foods, hydration, and avoiding smoking/recreational drugs rather than starting a condition-specific treatment based on online information.

It’s reasonable to seek a second opinion. Especially for major diagnoses or treatments, compare recommendations with another qualified clinician. Good medical care doesn’t require unquestioning trust.

Why You Should Read My Blog

This blog cannot prescribe your healthcare. But it can help you recognize patterns, evaluate claims and ask good questions of your healthcare provider with greater confidence. It’s not a tradeoff. Paired together, a blog can have good information, and your healthcare provider can help you determine what is right for you.

item.title: Happy-Loss: When the Nest Empties
item.description:
Parenting

Happy-Loss: When the Nest Empties

Feelings parents get when their kids leave home for the first time.

Posted August 17, 2026

Key points
  • Acknowledge your new empty nester's sadness: Give yourself permission to grieve.
  • Respect your child's boundaries: Allow them to become independent without allowing your anxiety to take over.
  • Trust your child: Trust what you taught them and learn to tolerate the unknown.
Image by Alisa Dyson from Pixabay
Source: Pixabay

"I'm so happy for you, but why am I crying?"

There are some parents who truly grieve over their children leaving home for the first time to attend college or other career opportunities. For others, it can be an emotionally taxing time for them. Instead of focusing on their feelings, other parents typically say things to them, such as:

  • "You should be happy that your kids are leaving.”
  • “Go on a vacation, you need to celebrate.”
  • “Good for you, I can’t wait until my kids leave.”
  • “You’re an empty nester.”

As a society, why don’t we focus on recent empty nesters’ feelings?

By the time our children become teenagers and enter 12th grade, many of us are ready for them to leave home, at least we think that we are ready. For various reasons, the teenage years can be a very challenging time for most parents. When a child is graduating from high school and ready to leave home for the first time, it’s no wonder why other parents are in awe of you and celebrating even if you do not feel like doing so – yet. Those other parents do not know the challenge of how it feels to know that your former little baby is going away for good – and that the relationship, the household, and your role as a parent will never be exactly the same again.

It’s “the same again” part that bothered me when my first child left home to attend college. Believe me, I can relate. The minute that I arrived home after dropping my child off to college, I was sad. Sad does not mean a lack of happiness for your child at all. It’s the start of their independent lives, which is worth celebrating; however, the change hurts your heart. It feels empty and confusing, and functioning again without that child’s daily presence is a new learning process. I had to find “me” again, and I will teach you how to do it.

  1. Acknowledge Your Sadness. Give yourself permission to grieve. Despite other parents' admiration of you for your new independence, stay within your feelings until they return to a typical response. This may last for a while and/or until the time that you see your child again. Unless you present with sadness that interferes in your daily living, I want you to grieve. You're not grieving because your child is gone, but because the way that you experience your child has changed, and that does hurt.
  2. Respect Their Boundaries. I know that you want to speak to and see your child, but if you have attended college or know what it’s like to leave home for the first time, you know it's important to respect their time. Try not to reduce your own anxiety by becoming an umbrella parent now that they are on their own. That’s not fair to them or you and does not allow them to become independent adults. For example, they need to learn how to solve problems on their own. They will let you know when you are needed and, believe me, you are the most important person to them in that time of need. Allow them some space to come to you.
  3. Trust Your Child: You raised them. I know you’re probably thinking, “It’s the world that I don’t trust,” and that’s completely understandable. But it's important to avoid pushing our anxiety onto them and allow them freedom so they can become productive adults. If you've been allowing them some freedom all along, by the time they're 18-years-old, you'll realize you were actually raising an adult in preparation for this moment! You did it!

Despite this pivotal moment in your life, others may still try to distract you from feelings of loss by saying things such as, “They will be just fine in college” or “You were fine when you left home” which always struck a nerve with me. For new empty nesters, I replace that with,

“Tell me what scares you the most?”

If I had to guess, the answer would be, the "unknown" or not knowing what they’re doing all of the time while they are not in your sight. I agree, that’s the scary part in this entire episode of emotions that new empty nesters feel. But you will come to terms with it. Trust your child until you have a reason not to do so, then you will react as needed. Parenting never stops, but changing how you parent does matter at this stage. Find other things to do with your newly found time that will allow you to decrease your worry.

  1. Find Your Balance: This is a very important step because finding your balance helps to restore your peace, which in turn, allows you to embrace the experience. Your parenting skills have allowed your child to attend college. That’s a huge milestone in both of your lives. Be proud of the adult that you have raised. Celebrate that your parenting skills, guidance, and wisdom have led them to pursue higher education and other careers. Parents do not give themselves enough credit, and this is your time to shine too. You are also a role model for other parents. You have learned the dos and don’ts of children leaving home for the first time. It’s perfectly fine to honor this journey even if you still feel sad at times. The key is to find the right balance to offset the sadness. Understand that not being sad does not mean that you care less about your child leaving home. What it means is that you are starting to adjust to the outcome of your parenting skills, and that’s a wonderful feeling.
  2. It’s a New Life, Embrace It. You must adjust and remove obstacles that get in the way of your own life satisfaction. Seek to find what else could be causing you not to embrace this new time in your life, such as:
  • The need for new and supportive friends
  • Watching social media posts of parents showing happiness as empty nesters
  • Needing to consult with therapists when sad, but avoiding it
  • Succumbing to negative comments from others

While finding balance, remember that sometimes sadness breeds negativity. If that’s the case, speak to a therapist who can help you. Your sadness can settle, especially if you remove things that may negatively affect your happiness.

Adulting is hard!

To find a therapist, visit the Psychology Today Therapy Directory.

item.title: What We Miss When We Mistake the Virtual for the Actual
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

What We Miss When We Mistake the Virtual for the Actual

Personal Perspective: AI can imitate speech, but not what actually makes relationships worthwhile.

Posted August 17, 2026

A chatbot can imitate a person, saying all the right things to a lonely teenager, but the best part of an actual relationship is missing—fellow feeling, emotions mutually expressed. A machine cannot emit emotion.

Another person alongside us can feel our feelings at a level beyond words. Much does not have to be spoken. There is nuance in the pauses, in moments when our tears start to form and we force them back in or release them. There are gestures—a hand placed lightly on an arm, a grimace from understanding something painful. Two people, speaker and listener, sense each other’s reactions, and a reflexive exchange ensues.

Nothing like this happens with a machine trained to provide a facsimile of presence. The AI persona offers the consolidated words millions of humans have used, an amalgam that sounds like sympathy but lacks feeling. There is no true exchange and the result is empty of what is actually needed. Dangerously, a vulnerable person—an insecure teenager, an adult in the midst of a crisis—who has retreated to the company of this kind of pseudo friend may come to think this is all there is.

The more people use chatbots, avatars, and robots, the more distant they become from what would genuinely sustain them. A homebound elder who talks to an avatar, a stand-in for a true companion, may not realize that accepting a ride to a weekly communal meal might have refreshed their spirit in a far more life-giving way. Images on screens, recorded voices, typed words and emojis are seductive representations, not what we really crave. All the ineffable qualities of human presence are missing.

Two good friends in-person
Source: Wendy Lustbader, 1982

Someone right there in front of us, responding in the moment to feelings of loss or joy, gives us something an amalgam can’t provide. When we are together with another person, it is possible to feel beheld. We may be able to say more than we thought we could or that we knew needed to be said. The other person’s facial expression, conveying interest, may draw us out. If we sense that this person is moved by what we are trying to describe, further feelings may arise in both people in the unison of discovery.

Artificial intelligence can generate plenty of words connoting emotion but cannot itself be moved. Lacking this deeply responsive dimension, it offers a mere approximation of emotional contact. Those who take solace from thinking they are being heard and understood may feel less lonely during interchanges with a chatbot, but isolation can expand insidiously through the blankness and distance of the surrogate.

Immediacy, presence, the primacy of feelings—maybe that’s why so many of us have dogs and cats, or prize proximity to children. They live in embodied time, which draws us in and must be heeded.

In-person emotion is visceral, specific to the fleeting moments that comprise our days. An actual friend has this crucial advantage over artificial intelligence. Anyone who has ever grieved in the presence of a caring other, human or animal, knows the difference. There is so much more to be gained, felt, and lived in real life.

Copyright: Wendy Lustbader, 2026

item.title: What Is Your Procrastination Trying to Protect You From?
item.description:
Procrastination

What Is Your Procrastination Trying to Protect You From?

The psychology behind putting things off.

Posted August 17, 2026

Key points
  • Procrastination goes beyond poor time management. It provides temporary relief from an uncomfortable emotion.
  • Procrastination may be driven by fear, perfectionism, or difficulty making distant goals feel real.
  • Shame tends to intensify the cycle.
  • Compassionate accountability helps clarify the protective function of delay while supporting forward movement.

You open your laptop to answer an important email. Before typing the first sentence, you decide to refill your water. Then you notice the dishes. Twenty minutes later, the kitchen counter is spotless, your inbox remains untouched, and a familiar voice has entered the room: Why do I always do this?

Procrastination often reflects an attempt to avoid a feeling. When a task triggers anxiety, boredom, self-doubt, or overwhelm, stepping away brings relief, and that relief reinforces the habit.

Choosing to wait or delay does not automatically qualify as procrastination. Deliberate delay can be thoughtful. Researchers generally define procrastination as voluntarily postponing an intended action despite expecting the delay to make matters worse.

Nine Ways of Getting Stuck

In his forthcoming book, Solving Procrastination: The Science of Why We Put Things Off and How to (Finally!) Stop, Dr. Itamar Shatz proposes nine procrastinator archetypes: the Worrier, Pessimist, Perfectionist, Dreamer, Zigzagger, Rebel, Thrill Seeker, Hedonist, and Burnout.

These archetypes function best as reflection tools rather than fixed personality types.

The framework challenges the assumption that every procrastinator needs the same solution. A calendar cannot resolve fear of failure. A motivational speech cannot restore a depleted nervous system. Removing a cellphone may help a Zigzagger, yet offer little benefit to a Rebel who experiences the task as an intrusion on autonomy.

Procrastination as Short-Term Mood Repair

One of the most important findings in procrastination research highlights delay as a form of immediate emotion regulation.

When a task evokes boredom, anxiety, confusion, inadequacy, resentment, or anticipated failure, stepping away produces a small but immediate mood improvement. The avoidance often targets the feeling associated with the task rather than the task itself.

Beginning may signal imperfection for a Perfectionist. A Worrier may anticipate uncertainty. A Rebel may resist feeling controlled. A Hedonist gravitates toward immediate rewards, while someone in burnout may lack the resources to initiate another demand.

Avoidance works briefly because stepping away reduces immediate discomfort. The nervous system learns that avoidance offers protection, reinforcing the pattern over time.

Relief fades quickly. The unfinished task lingers, while time pressure, guilt, and self-criticism build.

Discomfort → avoidance → temporary relief → increased pressure → self-criticism → greater discomfort → further avoidance

An Ancient Brain in an Abstract World

Shatz suggests that modern procrastination partly reflects a mismatch between systems tuned for immediate experience and a world filled with abstract, delayed consequences.

The nervous system mobilizes readily for what feels concrete and present. Modern life, however, requires tasks such as insurance paperwork, retirement planning, writing a dissertation, or sending tax documents whose benefits feel distant.

The discomfort of beginning arrives immediately. The benefit belongs to a future self who can feel psychologically remote.

Meanwhile, digital environments offer instant novelty and entertainment with minimal effort. A tax form resembles a beige wall, while a phone contains a thousand brightly lit doors.

Instead of asking, “How can I force myself to care more?” a more useful question becomes, “How can I make the next action clearer, safer, closer, and more immediately meaningful?”

Why the Inner Critic Fuels Procrastination: A Compassion-Focused Perspective

From a Compassion-Focused Therapy (CFT) perspective, the harsh voice, “You have no discipline. What is wrong with you?” reflects the inner critic, a threat-based system attempting to motivate change through pressure, shame, and fear.

CFT describes the mind as operating through a threat system focused on danger and protection, a drive system focused on achievement and reward, and a soothing system focused on safety, connection, and care.

During procrastination, the threat system often dominates, and the inner critic becomes one of its loudest expressions.

Many people try to overcome procrastination by amplifying this critic, hoping self-attack will generate urgency. While urgency may increase, so do threat, anxiety, and avoidance. When a task already feels overwhelming, added criticism further discourages engagement.

From this lens, procrastination involves avoiding both the task and the inner critic that emerges when engaging with it.

The Myth of Working Better Under Pressure

Some people complete tasks at the last minute and conclude that procrastination enhances performance.

A looming deadline can transform an abstract future consequence into an immediate one. Urgency narrows attention and temporarily overrides competing activities. However, completing the task does not show that waiting was the optimal strategy. Success may occur despite procrastination rather than because of it.

Deadline-driven work leaves little margin for illness, technical problems, caregiving emergencies, or thoughtful revision. Repeated reliance on crisis to generate motivation can gradually erode well-being.

While stress functions as an emergency response, it is not a sustainable productivity strategy.

A Compassionate Procrastination Reset

The next time you notice yourself circling a task, consider asking:

1. What feeling arrives immediately before I disengage?

Does boredom, uncertainty, resentment, fear of judgment, inadequacy, confusion, or exhaustion show up?

2. Is the task concrete enough to begin?

“Work on taxes” lacks specificity. “Download last year’s interest statement” provides a clear starting point.

3. How can I bring the future closer?

Use a ten-minute work interval, an accountability check, or connect the task to a present value.

4. What environmental change would make action easier?

Place the phone in another room. Work beside another person. Prepare materials in advance.

5. Am I avoiding discomfort, or am I genuinely depleted?

Someone experiencing burnout may need rest, reduced demands, support, or medical evaluation more than stricter scheduling. Difficulties with task initiation, attention, and time management can also occur alongside ADHD and other executive-function challenges.

From Self-Control to Self-Understanding

Procrastination reflects strategies for escaping discomfort, seeking stimulation, preserving autonomy, managing uncertainty, or conserving depleted resources.

These strategies often make sense in the short term, yet become costly over time.

The goal is to recover choice rather than achieve perfect productivity. Rest when rest supports well-being, delay when delay serves a purpose, and act when action aligns with what matters.

Progress begins by understanding what requires protection, then helping the mind and body find a less costly path forward.
